item.content:encoded: I got the impression that she already had suspicions before she interviewed her husband. Further, if it had invaded him, he would already be technically dead (a fact someone who had worked with 378 in the past would be aware of). So nobody is committing their husband to die. He's either already brain-dead, or he's safe.

item.content:encoded: Seeing one of my skips get a mention was a lovely surprise, but the rest left me, sadly, a little cold. I didn't actually like the characterisation much, or the bits in italics. It felt a bit contrived and unlikely. Also I don't like 378. Neutral vote, I think.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I really like the idea behind the characterization, but to be honest, it's slightly off. You overdo the freaking-out-almost-bursting-into-tears thing, and Nigel feels oddly characterized for the sake of making us wonder if he's the skip. (Though the idea there was good and it still works.)

Also you've got some odd style issues like — at the end of one scene — a pointless POV shift to Inglewood for one paragraph to info-dump his motives on us (and they also sound caricatured). Actually, while I like the idea of adding more misdirectional conflict, Inglewood seems like a caricature overall.

The section with the tests is excessively hard to follow due to lack of dialogue tags or any other indication of setting / scene-switching — had to read it a couple times for clarity. (Though, I'm sick, so maybe that didn't help.)

However… despite my issues, I found this all really quite compelling, which is the main thing I look for in a story, that can forgive any number of errors. Therefore, on balance, upvoting.

item.content:encoded:
I liked the Asimov reference but wish it was a little less heavy handed (do you really need an actually copy of "I, Robot" in the story?). I also wasn't crazy about the way of identifying the fake - if humans have worked on the Goldbach Conjecture for hundreds of years and haven't cracked it yet, how does a skip in 5 hours? I mean, I know it's anomalous, but as someone with a mathematical background, it irritates me.

I did like the characterization though. So, basically the exact opposite of what Kalinin said…

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I liked this. Kalinin's critique above is valid, and I agree with everything he said, but I was too impressed with the solution to not upvote this. Very clever. The prose is also, for like 95% of the time, solid work. Dialogue is engaging. I found the plot pretty interesting too. Characterization is solid.

Actually, I disagree with Kalinin's critique a bit. While the coincidence of the only specialist we have being the wife of one of the suspect five is, yeah, pretty contrived, I thought the depiction of the relationship was competently done. There's a certain tension in the dialogue in that the husband's words could have alternatively light-hearted or sinister implications and you never know until the end. Yeah, everything's a bit formulaic, but it's a well-executed formula.

In terms of things that I was not huge fans of, but were not big enough problems to make me downvote, I'd second the advice about "show, don't tell," and also object to Inglewood's flat characterization as "person who does not like the protagonist." Like, that's it. Why's he even in this story?

(ironically, i feel that this entry into the underappreciated articles contest is enormously underappreciated)

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I'm neutral voting this one. There are parts of the article that I really like. I enjoyed the skip that you used, and I liked the cleverness of the plan that the protagonist comes up with to identify the host. It's a good use of what I presume is a decent working background in mathematics. So despite my issues, I have no problem seeing this stick on the site.

I do have issues, though. There's parts of this where you should really let your writing do the work of telling the reader what's going on, rather than just flatly telling us. Example:

As Area 19's resident psychiatrist, he felt somewhat shafted by the decision to call her in. He was thus rather eager to prove himself.

I would much rather have seen this bit of information conveyed more through the character's attitude and actions; this approach lends itself, I find, to a richer and more satisfying reading experience.

Mostly, though, I don't care for the wife-husband thing you've got going in this story. Despite the somewhat convoluted reasoning that you gave up front, I still don't buy that they'd have someone so obviously compromised in a position where they might have to essentially kill their spouse, when the consequences of failure would be as high as they are here. The interactions between the two also don't ring especially true to me as a long-term married couple placed in repeated stressful situations. I'm not saying it needs to be overly dramatic, humorless grimdark, but there's a certain lightheartedness underlying the relationship that strikes an odd note in comparison to the situation.
